title: The passive: present and past
tagline: When the action matters more than who did it.
why: English uses the passive whenever the action matters more than who did it — in museum notices, news reports, instructions and formal writing, all of which appear in B1 Preliminary Reading and Writing. Choosing between the present and past passive, and deciding whether to add by + agent, is tested directly in the open cloze and rewarded in a well-written article or story.

hook.text: At the museum, Miss Vega says: "This vase was made in Cusco 500 years ago. Nobody knows who made it, so we just say it was made by a skilled Inca artist." Mateo: "So the vase is displayed here because it's so old?"
hook.ask: Miss Vega doesn't always say who did the action. Find the sentences where the subject RECEIVES the action instead of doing it. What form of be do they use?

diagrams.title: Active → passive

before.text: An Inca artist made this vase.

after.text: This vase was made by an Inca artist.

steps: The object of the active sentence (this vase) becomes the subject.
Add the correct form of be + past participle (was made).
Add by + the doer only if it's useful information.

use.point: Present passive: routines and general facts

examples.note: a general fact about the process
we know when, not always who
the object (paintings) is the focus, not the thief

examples.text: I was told not to touch the exhibits.
examples.note: someone told me — the doer isn't important here

examples.text: The vase was made by a famous Inca artist.
examples.note: by + agent when the doer is interesting
no by — we don't care who cleans it

examples.text: The museum was designed by a Peruvian architect.
examples.note: by + agent gives extra, useful information

use.point: Questions, negatives and present perfect passive

examples.text: This exhibition has been visited by thousands of people.
examples.note: present perfect passive: has/have been + participle

watch_out.why: The passive always needs a form of be — never the participle alone.

watch_out.wrong: The museum is closing on Mondays.
watch_out.why: Is closing is active/continuous; the passive fact needs is closed.

watch_out.wrong: The letter was wrote by Sofia.
watch_out.why: Use the past participle (written), not the past simple (wrote), after be.

watch_out.wrong: By an artist, the vase was made.
watch_out.right: The vase was made by an artist.
watch_out.why: By + agent goes at the end of the sentence, not the front.
A finished date in the past needs the past passive, not the present.
The present perfect passive needs been before the participle.

l1.why: The subject (Spanish) must come before is spoken — English can't start the sentence with the verb.
English needs the past participle (built) after was, not the base or infinitive form.

l1.wrong: I was said to arrive early.
l1.why: Say cannot be used in the passive with a person as the subject — use tell/told.

l1.wrong: The painting robbed it last night.
l1.why: Spanish can hide the passive inside an active sentence with se or lo; English needs be + participle and no extra pronoun.

remember.trick: No BE, no passive — that's the rule!
remember.tip: Find the form of be first (is, was, has been…) — the past participle always comes right after it.

can_do: I can use the present and past passive to talk about facts, processes and finished actions.
I can decide when to add by + the doer and when to leave it out.
I can make passive questions and negatives, including with the present perfect.
summary: Passive = be + past participle; the subject receives the action instead of doing it.
Present passive (is/are + participle) is for routines, facts and processes.
Past passive (was/were + participle) is for finished actions in the past.
Add by + agent only when the doer is interesting or important information.
Present perfect passive: has/have been + participle.
